newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton set for pre-APEC relaxation in Australia.
newsitem.headline: Clinton set for pre-APEC relaxation in Australia.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton kicks off his first overseas trip on Tuesday since his re-election with a five-day working holiday in Australia.

Clinton's first official visit to a key U.S. ally in the Pacific will feature a meeting with Prime Minister John Howard, a speech to parliament and an address to the people of Australia from a cove near the Sydney Opera House.
But Clinton will also take time out to play a round or two of golf and try to recover from the rigours of his long re-election campaign.
Accompanied by his wife Hillary, Clinton will round off the visit with two days on the north Queensland coast and the Great Barrier Reef, one of the world's most famous beauty spots.
Clinton's visit is the first leg of a 12-day regional trip centreing on a November 25 summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Manila and including a visit to Thailand.
In Manila, Clinton will meet Asian heavyweights such as Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.

By comparison, Australia is seen as a second-tier regional player -- and its leaders will be monitoring Clinton's every remark to gauge his views on the future of the Asia-Pacific and the United States' and Australia's roles within it.

A developed country of 18 million people, Australia is accustomed to punching above its weight on the diplomatic front. It played a leading role, for example, in reviving the nuclear test ban treaty at the United Nations in September.

But Australia's unexpected failure to secure a non-permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council last month battered the pride of its diplomatic corps and Clinton's high-profile visit is seen as a chance to lift morale.
Howard, who came to power in March at the head of a conservative coalition, will spend an hour with Clinton on Wednesday at Parliament House in Canberra.

Australian officials said last week bilateral trade issues would feature heavily in Clinton's visit -- grain subsidies and a trade dispute involving Australian leather exports are two points of contention between Canberra and Washington.
But Howard may prefer to keep trade rows out of the meeting to try to develop the kind of personal rapport with Clinton enjoyed by his left-wing predecessor Paul Keating.

After a day in Canberra, during which Clinton will become only the second U.S. president after George Bush to address both houses of parliament, the U.S. leader and his party will enjoy a dinner cruise on Sydney harbour on Wednesday evening.
On Thursday, Clinton will address the people of Australia from a cove near the Opera House and the First Lady will speak to some of Australia's most influential women inside the building.

Clinton is also expected to play a round of golf on Thursday. New U.S. star Tiger Woods and Australia's world number one Greg Norman are both playing in a Sydney tournament at the time and either would provide the perfect partner.

That evening, the Clinton entourage will fly up Australia's east coast to the Queensland town of Port Douglas, where all 392 rooms and villas of an exclusive Barrier Reef resort have been booked to accommodate them.
Apart from making a speech on the environment, the Clintons will have two full days to relax and enjoy Australia's tropical north before heading to the Philippines.
